# Worked examples: spreadsheets {#sec-examples-spreadsheet}


::: {.cell}

:::


These examples use only the aggregate tables and a spreadsheet. The steps are
written for Excel; other spreadsheets work the same way. The results shown
were calculated from the same files, so you can check your answer against
them.

## Example 1: average car mileage by postcode area

**Question:** How far is the average car driven in each postcode area, and
which areas have the highest and lowest mileage?

**File:** `tables/mileage/mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv`

**Steps:**

1. Open the file and insert a PivotTable (Insert › PivotTable).
2. Add `year` and `body_type` to **Filters**, and choose `2022` and `Cars`.
   (2022 rather than a later year: see @sec-pitfalls, pitfall 2.)
3. Add `pca` to **Rows**. Then use the row filter to untick `unborn`,
   `unknown`, `dead` and `XX`, which are not postcode areas.
4. Add `total_legit_mileage` and `n_legit_mileage` to **Values**, both as
   *Sum*.
5. Next to the PivotTable, divide the first sum by the second to get average
   miles per car. (Or add a *Calculated Field*: PivotTable Analyze › Fields,
   Items & Sets › Calculated Field, with the formula
   `= total_legit_mileage / n_legit_mileage`.)
6. Sort by the average.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::


**Result:** the national average is
6,623 miles per car.

::: {layout-ncol=2}

::: {#tbl-ex1-high .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Highest average car mileage, 2022'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Area                  | Cars with plausible mileage| Miles per car|
|:---------------------|---------------------------:|-------------:|
|Northern Ireland (BT) |                     967,427|         7,910|
|Luton (LU)            |                     204,075|         7,411|
|Perth (PH)            |                      96,561|         7,272|
|Galashiels (TD)       |                      59,640|         7,230|
|Peterborough (PE)     |                     593,022|         7,190|


:::
:::



::: {#tbl-ex1-low .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Lowest average car mileage, 2022'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Area                      | Cars with plausible mileage| Miles per car|
|:-------------------------|---------------------------:|-------------:|
|Sutton (SM)               |                      69,753|         5,215|
|South West London (SW)    |                     171,424|         5,250|
|Bromley (BR)              |                     132,826|         5,299|
|South East London (SE)    |                     257,119|         5,622|
|Kingston upon Thames (KT) |                     296,399|         5,625|


:::
:::

:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::


::: {.callout-important title="The wrong way"}
Each row of the file is one fuel group in one area. If instead you add a
column of averages for each row and take the average of that column, every
row counts equally, including rows of a handful of fuel cell cars. Done that
way, the "national average" comes out at 7,198 miles rather
than 6,623. Always sum totals and counts first, then divide.
:::

**Interpreting it:** low averages in London, and high ones in more rural
areas, are what you would expect. Northern Ireland, at the top, is tested
differently from Great Britain (@sec-pitfalls, pitfall 11), so compare it with
care. Remember that these are cars *tested*
in each area (@sec-geography), that each postcode area mixes very different
places, and that taxis and private hire cars, which are driven far further,
are concentrated in cities.

## Example 2: the share of electric cars

**Question:** Where is the share of battery electric cars highest?

**File:** the same as Example 1.

**Steps:**

1. In the same PivotTable (year 2022, Cars, status rows removed), remove the
   mileage values and add `n_vehicles` to **Values** as *Sum*.
2. Add `fuel_simple` to **Columns**. Each area now has a count for each fuel
   and a grand total.
3. Next to the PivotTable, divide the `Electric` column by the grand total.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::



::: {#tbl-ex2 .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Postcode areas with the highest share of battery electric cars among cars observed, 2022'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Area                      |    Cars| Electric| Share|
|:-------------------------|-------:|--------:|-----:|
|North West London (NW)    | 271,700|   13,170|  4.8%|
|West London (W)           | 109,560|    5,060|  4.6%|
|Watford (WD)              | 169,470|    5,190|  3.1%|
|Milton Keynes (MK)        | 399,926|   11,479|  2.9%|
|South West London (SW)    | 193,803|    5,275|  2.7%|
|Oxford (OX)               | 412,086|   10,695|  2.6%|
|Kingston upon Thames (KT) | 325,283|    8,367|  2.6%|
|St Albans (AL)            | 171,905|    4,381|  2.5%|


:::
:::


**Result:** nationally, 1.6% of the cars observed in 2022 were
battery electric.

::: {.callout-important title="Why this understates electric cars"}
Most electric cars are new, and a new car has no location until its first
MOT at three years old. An electric car bought in 2021 is filled in back to
2021 once it is tested in 2024, but one bought in 2023 is not in the data at
all yet. The share among cars *observed* is therefore well below the share among
cars *registered*; for current figures on the newest vehicles use DfT's
statistics (table VEH0135 or VEH0145), and use CARS for what happens to
electric cars once they are three or more. Some areas also have high shares
because of company fleets and leasing companies tested there.
:::

## Example 3: the fleet by Euro standard

**Question:** How has the share of cars meeting each Euro standard changed?

**File:** `tables/profile/a1_counts_cars.csv`. This is a wide table: one row
per year, and one column for each category of each characteristic, named
`characteristic: category`.

**Steps:**

1. Open the file. Hide or delete the columns you don't need, keeping `year`
   and the `euro_standard: ...` columns.
2. Add a column adding up the Euro standard columns for each year, and
   divide each column by it to get shares.
3. Select the year column and the share columns, and insert a line chart.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Share of cars by Euro standard, among cars with a plausible mileage in Great Britain. Most Euro standards are assumed from the date of manufacture (@sec-fuels-emissions).](examples-spreadsheet_files/figure-html/fig-ex3-1.png){#fig-ex3 fig-align='center' width=1050}
:::
:::


**Interpreting it:** the chart shows each standard rising as new cars meet it
and falling as those cars age and leave the fleet. The profile tables count
only cars with a plausible mileage that year, and exclude Northern Ireland.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

:::


::: {.callout-important title="Spotting a problem: Euro 6 cars in 2005"}
The chart shows 0.2% of cars as Euro 6 in 2005, nearly ten years
before the standard existed. These are not real. They are cars whose Euro
status was missing and was filled from similar vehicles (the same make, model,
birth year and fuel), where a single wrong value recorded for one vehicle was
copied to the rest of its group. The vehicle table flags them with
`euro_check = 'later_than_date'`.

This is a good example of why you should check where values come from before
relying on them. Most Euro standards in the data are filled or assumed rather
than recorded; the `euro_source: ...` columns of the same table show how many
of each. For a defensible analysis of Euro standards, use the vehicle table and
exclude or correct values flagged `later_than_date` (@sec-pitfalls,
pitfall 7).
:::
